qs.q: A pathology report describes atypical lobular hyperplasia in a breast biopsy specimen. Which histological criterion distinguishes atypical lobular hyperplasia from lobular carcinoma in situ?
o: Cells filling less than 50% of the acini within a single lobule
Presence of prominent branching fibrovascular cores within the acini
Dyscohesive cells with loss of E-cadherin expression
Complete architectural effacement of the entire terminal duct lobular unit
qs.e: Atypical lobular hyperplasia and lobular carcinoma in situ share identical dyscohesive cells with loss of E-cadherin, but ALH cells fill less than 50% of the acini in a lobule while LCIS fills more than 50%. Both lesions represent proliferative disease with atypia.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH) is a proliferative lesion of breast lobules with some, but not all, features of lobular carcinoma in situ. It signals an increased risk of developing invasive breast cancer.

b: Often asymptomatic; may be discovered with a palpable mass or imaging abnormality
Considered a high‑risk lesion, not cancer itself
sections.p: ALH is a clonal expansion of lobular epithelial cells showing partial loss of E‑cadherin and mild cytologic atypia. It is usually found incidentally on core needle biopsy.

t.b: Does the lesion meet criteria for ALH vs. LCIS? → Confirms diagnosis and guides management
Is E‑cadherin lost? → Supports lobular lineage; loss is typical in ALH/LCIS
What is the extent of disease? → Detects associated calcifications or masses; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam and risk assessment

b: Diagnostic criteria: ≤ 50 % of acini involved, partial loss of E‑cadherin, mild nuclear atypia
Risk: 4‑5‑fold increase in invasive carcinoma compared with general population
Management depends on patient age, family history, and imaging findings
sections.p: ALH represents a spectrum of lobular neoplasia; it is a marker of future cancer risk rather than an invasive tumor.

b: Discuss chemoprevention (e.g., selective estrogen receptor modulators) for high‑risk women
Consider MRI screening if dense breast tissue or strong family history
Surgical excision only if imaging shows a residual mass or if pathology is discordant
sections.p: Patients with ALH need individualized risk‑reduction strategies and careful surveillance because they may progress to ductal or lobular carcinoma.

b: ALH involves ≤ 50 % of lobular units; LCIS involves > 50 %
Both lack E‑cadherin; loss helps differentiate from ductal lesions
Management is risk‑based, not excision of every lesion
sections.p: Focus on distinguishing ALH from LCIS, recognizing its risk implications, and outlining appropriate follow‑up.

b: Assuming ALH requires mastectomy – it does not
Missing the need for long‑term surveillance
Confusing ALH with fibroadenoma on imaging
sections.p: Students often treat ALH as cancer or overlook its risk‑stratification role.
